clinicalPearls: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP, extrinsic allergic alveolitis) results from inhalational exposure to a wide range of antigens, producing an inflammatory response of the alveoli and small airways; systemic symptoms such as fever and fatigue can accompany the respiratory complaints (p.2228).
Sensitization to an inhaled antigen (specific circulating IgG) is necessary but NOT sufficient to define HP, because many sensitized individuals never develop disease (p.2228-2229).
There is an as-yet-unexplained DECREASED risk of developing HP in smokers (p.2229).

US risk groups include farmers (farmer's lung: thermophilic actinomycetes/Aspergillus from grain, moldy hay, silage), bird owners (bird fancier's lung: feather, dropping and serum-protein antigens), industrial workers (chemical worker's lung: diphenylmethane and toluene diisocyanate), and hot tub users; mycobacteria can cause HP rather than frank infection in hot tub lung and metalworking-fluid HP (p.2229).

Recent guidelines advocate ABANDONING the acute/subacute/chronic terminology in favor of categorizing HP as either nonfibrotic or fibrotic; cluster analysis splits patients into a recurrent-systemic-symptom group and a more-severe-respiratory group (p.2229).
Antigen avoidance generally results in resolution of symptoms; acute symptoms may resolve within hours to days, while a more subacute course resolves over weeks to months (p.2229).

Chronic/fibrotic HP can present insidiously with progressive dyspnea, cough, fatigue, weight loss and digital clubbing, and-unlike other forms-can have an irreversible respiratory component NOT responsive to antigen removal; bird-antigen exposure tends toward a fibrotic phenotype while farmer's lung may show an emphysematous phenotype (p.2229).

Diagnosis depends foremost on a history of exposure to an offending antigen that correlates with symptoms; a careful occupational and home exposure history is essential and may be supplemented by a clinician visit to the work or home environment, with reexposure sometimes used to confirm the diagnosis (p.2229).
BAL lymphocytosis is characteristic of HP though not specific; most cases have a CD4+/CD8+ ratio <1, but a lower lymphocyte threshold should be applied in active smokers (p.2230).

Characteristic HP histology is loose, poorly defined NONcaseating granulomas near small airways-contrasting with the well-formed granulomas of sarcoidosis-plus a patchy lymphocyte-predominant interstitial infiltrate and bronchiolitis with organizing exudate (p.2230).

HP Study Group clinical prediction rule: six significant predictors, the strongest being exposure to a known HP antigen; others are serum precipitins, recurrent symptoms, symptoms 4-8 h after exposure, inspiratory crackles, and weight loss (p.2230).

Pulmonary eosinophilic syndromes share pulmonary infiltrates plus increased eosinophils in tissue, sputum and/or BAL; the first classifying step is distinguishing PRIMARY disorders from eosinophilia SECONDARY to a drug, infection, malignancy, or another pulmonary condition such as asthma (p.2231).

Acute eosinophilic pneumonia (AEP): acute febrile illness <1 month with hypoxemic respiratory failure (often needing ventilation), diffuse infiltrates and BAL eosinophilia >25%; typically affects men aged 20-40 with NO asthma history and is often linked to recent tobacco initiation, vaping, or dust from indoor renovation (p.2231).

AEP is often initially mistaken for acute lung injury/ARDS until BAL reveals >25% eosinophils; peripheral eosinophilia is often ABSENT at presentation but appears 7-30 days later; it is distinguished by absence of organ failure beyond the lungs, high corticosteroid responsiveness, excellent prognosis, and recovery without relapse (p.2231-2232).

Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia (CEP): indolent illness, mostly female nonsmokers (mean age 45), many with asthma; the 'photographic negative of pulmonary edema' (peripheral/pleural-based opacities) is pathognomonic but seen in <25% of patients; ~90% have peripheral eosinophilia and >50% relapse, often needing prolonged corticosteroids (p.2232).

EGPA (formerly Churg-Strauss): eosinophilic vasculitis with asthma and multi-organ involvement (lung, heart, skin, GI, nerve, kidney); peripheral eosinophilia >1000/uL (or >10% WBC) and ANCA (perinuclear/anti-MPO) in about one-third of patients; cardiac, GI and renal involvement portend a poorer prognosis (p.2232-2233).

ABPA is an eosinophilic disorder from allergic sensitization to Aspergillus, presenting asthmatically with brownish mucus plugs; it features prominent peripheral eosinophilia, IgE >500 (often >1000) IU/mL, and Aspergillus sensitivity-central bronchiectasis is a classic finding but is NOT required for diagnosis; consider ABPA in refractory asthma and as a complication of cystic fibrosis (p.2233-2234).

Loffler syndrome is transient pulmonary infiltrates with eosinophilia from helminthic larvae passing through the lung, most commonly Ascaris (also hookworm); symptoms are generally self-limited (p.2234).
harrison.pathophysiology: HP is an immune-mediated reaction to inhaled antigens small enough to deposit in distal airways and alveoli, characterized by dysregulated TH1 and TH17 responses. Precipitating IgG antibodies indicate adaptive immunity, but innate mechanisms also contribute, with Toll-like receptors and downstream MyD88 signaling driving neutrophil recruitment. No clear genetic basis is established, though polymorphisms in antigen-processing genes (TAP1, MHC class II) occur in some cohorts. In chronic HP, bone marrow-derived fibrocytes may contribute to inflammation and fibrosis, and chronic HP shares the MUC5B promoter polymorphism with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. In the pulmonary eosinophilic syndromes, the eosinophil is central; pathology shows tissue eosinophil infiltration, and in EGPA extravascular granulomas and necrotizing vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosis/thrombosis may involve lung, heart, skin, muscle, liver, spleen and kidney. These syndromes are thought to arise from dysregulated eosinophilopoiesis or autoimmunity (elevated IgE, IgG4, rheumatoid factor; heightened T-cell immunity); IL-5 is hypothesized to be etiologic, and ANCAs binding vascular walls likely contribute to vascular injury in EGPA (p.2229, 2231).
additionalDifferentials: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) - hard to distinguish from fibrotic HP even on biopsy; in HP the lung bases are frequently spared
Sarcoidosis - distinguished by prominent hilar adenopathy, extrapulmonary involvement and well-formed noncaseating granulomas
Organic toxic dust syndrome (OTDS) - neither requires prior sensitization nor shows specific IgG antibodies
Acute lung injury / ARDS (mimicked by acute eosinophilic pneumonia)
Hypereosinophilic syndromes (HES) and EGPA when nonrespiratory features accompany an eosinophilic pneumonia
infectionMimics: Respiratory infection (nonfibrotic HP can be mistaken for it)
Loffler syndrome from Ascaris or hookworm larvae
Strongyloides stercoralis (chronic infection and, in immunocompromised/steroid-treated hosts, fatal hyperinfection)
Paragonimiasis, filariasis (tropical eosinophilia from Wuchereria), visceral larval migrans
Nonparasitic infections: coccidioidomycosis, paracoccidioidomycosis, basidiobolomycosis, tuberculosis
nonInfectiousMimics: Drug/toxin reaction (NSAIDs, systemic antibiotics, particulate metals, inhalational drugs of abuse, post-radiation pneumonitis)
Malignancy-associated eosinophilia (leukemia, lymphoma, lung cancer, adenocarcinoma/squamous cell carcinoma)
additionalInvestigations: Careful occupational/home/avocational exposure history (cornerstone of HP diagnosis), possibly with site visit
HRCT: ground-glass opacities and centrilobular nodules in nonfibrotic HP, expiratory air trapping; reticular changes/traction bronchiectasis and basal-sparing honeycombing in fibrotic HP
Pulmonary function tests (restrictive OR obstructive; not diagnostic but track impairment and response; DLCO may be markedly reduced in fibrotic HP)
Serum precipitins / specific IgG to suspected antigens (presence alone insufficient; limited panels give false negatives)
Bronchoscopy with BAL (lymphocytosis, CD4/CD8 <1 in most)
Lung biopsy (transbronchial, cryobiopsy, or surgical) for noncaseating granulomas - not absolutely required

For eosinophilic syndromes: blood eosinophil count, BAL eosinophil percentage (>25% in AEP; ~60% mean in CEP), ESR/CRP/IgE, ANCA (anti-MPO in EGPA), and as needed echocardiogram, electromyogram, bone marrow biopsy
ABPA: total IgE (>500, often >1000 IU/mL), Aspergillus skin test/specific IgE, Aspergillus precipitins/specific IgG, chest imaging for central bronchiectasis and mucus impaction
redFlags: Hypoxemic respiratory failure with diffuse infiltrates in a previously healthy young man - consider acute eosinophilic pneumonia
Progressive dyspnea, weight loss and digital clubbing with honeycombing - chronic/fibrotic HP that may be irreversible and IPF-like

Asthma with neuropathy (mononeuritis multiplex), purpura, cardiac or renal involvement and eosinophilia - EGPA; cardiac involvement portends worse prognosis and up to 50% of untreated EGPA die within 3 months
Refractory asthma with brownish mucus plugs and very high IgE - evaluate for ABPA
Eosinophilia in an immunocompromised or steroid-treated patient - risk of fatal Strongyloides hyperinfection
harrison.prognosis: HP that has not progressed to chronic lung disease has a favorable outcome with likely resolution if antigen avoidance is achieved; chronic HP with lung fibrosis has a poorer prognosis, with chronic pigeon breeder's lung showing mortality similar to IPF. Acute eosinophilic pneumonia has an excellent prognosis with near-complete recovery and no recurrence. Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia responds rapidly to corticosteroids but >50% of patients relapse. In EGPA, up to 50% of untreated patients die within 3 months of diagnosis whereas treated patients have >70% six-year survival; clinical remission is achievable in >90% with ~25% relapsing, and myocardial, GI and renal involvement portend a poor prognosis. HES respond less reliably to corticosteroids (<50% first-line responders) (p.2229, 2232, 2233).
pitfalls: Failing to obtain a detailed exposure history - the single most important step, as the strongest HP predictor is exposure to a known antigen
Relying on specific IgG/precipitins alone: asymptomatic exposed individuals (farmers, pigeon breeders) can be IgG positive, and limited antigen panels often yield false negatives
Expecting a particular PFT pattern - HP can be restrictive OR obstructive, so PFTs do not establish the diagnosis
Misdiagnosing AEP as ARDS/acute lung injury because peripheral eosinophilia is often absent at presentation (BAL eosinophilia is the key)
Treating EGPA-prone severe asthma with corticosteroids can mask systemic eosinophilia and vasculitis and delay the EGPA diagnosis
Confusing fibrotic HP with IPF/NSIP even on biopsy (basal sparing favors HP)
harrison.severityClassification: Current guidance categorizes HP as nonfibrotic versus fibrotic (replacing the older acute/subacute/chronic scheme). Acute eosinophilic pneumonia diagnostic criteria: acute febrile respiratory illness <1 month, hypoxemic respiratory failure, diffuse infiltrates on chest x-ray, BAL eosinophilia >25%, absence of parasitic/fungal/other infection, absence of drugs known to cause pulmonary eosinophilia, quick corticosteroid response, and failure to relapse after stopping corticosteroids.
